name: Boethius

seo.title: Boethius: the Consolation of Philosophy, his death and his quotes
seo.description: Who Boethius was, in plain words: the book he wrote in prison, how he died, why Pavia calls him a saint, and his words with the book and chapter.

band.lede: A Roman statesman and philosopher, who wrote his great book in prison while he waited to die.

picture.alt: An engraving of Boethius as a Roman in a toga: a clean-shaven man with short curly hair, looking straight out, his right hand raised and a scroll in his left
picture.credit: Boethius, an imagined likeness, André Thevet, Les vrais pourtraits et vies des hommes illustres, 1584. Public domain.
picture.creator: André Thevet

card.line: A Roman statesman and philosopher, who wrote his great book in prison while he waited to die.

who: Boethius was a Roman senator and scholar in Italy, under the Gothic king Theodoric. He put Aristotle's logic into Latin, and the West learned it from him for centuries. He rose to head the king's civil service. Then he was accused of treason, condemned unheard, and killed. In prison he wrote The *Consolation of Philosophy*.

lines: He gave the speech praising the king that day
“Near five hundred miles away”, he says

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 480, at **Rome**. Some scholars say a few years earlier. No ancient source gives the year.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: In Rome, in the old family of the **Anicii**. His father, consul in 487, died when he was a child. The senator **Symmachus** raised him, and he married Symmachus's daughter, **Rusticiana**.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: In **524**, or perhaps 526, near **Pavia** in northern Italy. King Theodoric had him put to death without a hearing.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: At Pavia, in the church of **San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro**, St Peter in the Golden Sky. The bones of St Augustine lie in the same church.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: His full name was **Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius**. At Pavia he is **St Severinus Boethius**, San Severino Boezio in Italian.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A local saint for Catholics, honoured at Pavia as a martyr. He is not in the Church's general calendar. The Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans do not keep him.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A scholar in a cap, often in prison or in bed, with **Lady Philosophy** beside him. In his book she holds a notebook and a staff. The wheel of Fortune often turns nearby.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: **The Consolation of Philosophy**, in five books. Five short works of theology, one of them doubted. Latin translations of Aristotle's logic and of Porphyry, with commentaries. Textbooks on arithmetic and music.

portrait.alt: A Renaissance portrait of Boethius as a grave, middle-aged scholar in a white cap, a green gown and a red hood. He sits with his hands raised as if counting points, with a closed book beside him. The name FL BOETIO is painted below.
portrait.credit: Fl Boetio (Boethius), Justus van Gent and Pedro Berruguete, about 1472-1476. Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, Urbino. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Justus van Gent and Pedro Berruguete
portrait.caption: Painted about 1472 to 1476 for the study of Federico da Montefeltro at Urbino, in a row of famous men. The name below reads FL BOETIO. Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, Urbino. Public domain.

west.text: **Catholic**, at Pavia, where his church keeps it as a solemnity. Also in today's **Roman Martyrology**, which names him a martyr. The 1916 edition does not list him. Not in the General Roman Calendar.

feasts.note: No Orthodox calendar keeps him. Neither do the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, the **Missouri Synod** or the **ELCA**. No source says why 23 October, and no ancient source gives the day he died.

traits.title: honest about what he did not know
traits.text: At a meeting, a letter from Eastern bishops to the Pope was read out. It asked about Christ's two natures. Everyone loudly said the answer was obvious, but no one really answered it. Boethius admits he had no answer either. The difference was that he lacked “the false assumption of a knowledge that I had not got”. So he held his peace and thought it through, “chewing the cud of constant meditation”. The result was his treatise *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*.

cite.text: Against Eutyches and Nestorius, preface, with the Loeb note

traits.title: no friend to the powerful
traits.text: He says he went into public life to put philosophy into practice, and it made him enemies. He stood up to the king's officials when they preyed on the weak. When a forced sale in a time of famine threatened Campania with starvation, he fought it before the king and stopped it. “I have had to think nothing of giving offence to the powerful in the cause of justice.”

cite.text: Consolation of Philosophy, Book 1, prose 4

traits.title: a lover of music
traits.text: When Clovis, king of the Franks, asked for a harper, King Theodoric turned to Boethius to choose one, “because you, being such a lover of music yourself, will be able to introduce us to the right man”. His own textbook on music, say his Loeb translators, “was in use at Oxford and Cambridge until modern times”.

cite.text: Cassiodorus, Variae, Book 2, letter 40; Stewart and Rand, Introduction

traits.title: wrote for the few
traits.text: He wrote his treatise on the Trinity for his father-in-law, in hard, new words, on purpose. He said so plainly: “The rest of the world I simply disregard: they cannot understand, and therefore do not deserve to read.”

cite.text: On the Trinity, preface

said.lede: He was praised in his own day, even by the king who later had him killed, and for centuries after.

quotes.q: You have thoroughly imbued yourself with Greek philosophy. You have translated Pythagoras the musician, Ptolemy the astronomer, Nicomachus the arithmetician, Euclid the geometer, Plato the theologian, Aristotle the logician, and have given back the mechanician Archimedes to his own Sicilian countrymen (who now speak Latin).
quotes.who: King Theodoric, in a letter written for him by Cassiodorus

cite.text: Cassiodorus, Variae, Book 1, letter 45

quotes.q: …because they practised philosophy and were mindful of justice in a manner surpassed by no other men, relieving the destitution of both citizens and strangers by generous gifts of money, they attained great fame and thus led men of the basest sort to envy them.
quotes.who: Procopius, a historian of the next generation, on Boethius and his father-in-law Symmachus

cite.text: History of the Wars, Book 5, chapter 1

quotes.q: The sainted soul, which the fallacious world / Makes manifest to him who listeneth well; / The body whence ’twas hunted forth is lying / Down in Cieldauro, and from martyrdom / And banishment it came unto this peace.
quotes.who: Dante, about eight hundred years later. He places him in heaven among the wise, without naming him. Cieldauro is his church at Pavia.

cite.text: Paradiso, Canto 10, tr. Longfellow

moments.title: An orphan in a great house
moments.text: His father, a former consul, died when he was small. He grew up in the house of Symmachus, a senator admired for his character and learning. Later he married Symmachus's daughter, Rusticiana. In his prison book, Philosophy reminds him how, “when orphaned and desolate, thou wast taken into the care of illustrious men”.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 3; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: Greek into Latin
moments.text: He set out to put all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, with notes. He never finished, but he translated much of Aristotle's logic, and wrote textbooks on arithmetic and music. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says the medieval schools, down to the twelfth century, “depended entirely on Boethius for their knowledge of Aristotle's doctrines”.

cite.text: Stewart and Rand, Introduction; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: Clocks for a king
moments.text: King Theodoric used his learning in diplomacy. He asked him to have a water-clock and a sundial made, as a gift for the king of the Burgundians. “Exert yourself therefore, oh Boetius, to get this thing put in hand,” the king wrote.

cite.text: Cassiodorus, Variae, Book 1, letter 45

moments.title: Two sons, two consuls
moments.text: He had been consul himself in 510, holding the office alone. In 522 his two young sons were made consuls together. They rode out with a train of senators behind them. In the senate house he gave the speech praising the king. Then he sat between his sons at the Circus and handed out gifts to the crowd. In his prison book, Philosophy says Fortune gave him “a boon which she had never before granted to any private person”. That year the king made him Master of Offices, head of the civil service.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 3; James, Proem

moments.title: Standing with Albinus
moments.text: An informer, Cyprian, accused the senator Albinus of writing to the emperor at Constantinople against the king. Boethius spoke up for him in the king's presence: “The charge of Cyprianus is false, but if Albinus did that, so also have I and the whole senate with one accord done it; it is false, my Lord King.” Cyprian then brought false witnesses against Boethius too, and the king believed them.

cite.text: Anonymus Valesianus, part 2, sections 85 and 86; Consolation, Book 1, prose 4

moments.title: Condemned unheard
moments.text: He and Albinus were locked in a church's baptistery. Later he was held on an estate near Pavia. The king had him sentenced without a hearing. Boethius says the senate itself passed decrees against him. Besides treason, “they falsely asserted that in the pursuit of my ambition I had stained my conscience with sacrilegious acts”. In prison, waiting to die, he wrote The *Consolation of Philosophy*.

cite.text: Anonymus Valesianus, part 2, section 87; Consolation, Book 1, prose 4

extras.title: Who is Lady Philosophy?
extras.lede: She is not a real woman. She is Philosophy herself, the love of wisdom, pictured as a woman. She is the other voice in the book Boethius wrote in prison, *The Consolation of Philosophy*. She talks, scolds and comforts him like a real teacher, so she is easy to take for one.

items.title: An idea with a voice
items.text: Boethius tells the book as if it really happened, and he plays himself in it. Philosophy comes to him in the form of a woman, much as Justice is pictured today as a woman holding scales. She is an idea given a voice, not a visitor. He gives Fortune a voice in the same way, in Book 2. The *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* calls the book “an imagined dialogue between the prisoner Boethius and a lady who personifies Philosophy”. He tells of her coming like a vision:
items.quote: it seemed to me that there appeared above my head a woman of a countenance exceeding venerable.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 1; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

items.title: How he pictures her
items.text: He describes her with care. She seems very old, yet full of strength. Her eyes blaze, keener than any human eye. Her robe is one she wove with her own hands, dulled now by age and neglect. On its hem is the Greek letter P, and at its top the letter Th. Steps like a staircase climb from one to the other. Her English translator, H. R. James, explains the letters in a note: P for the life of action, Th for the life of thought. She holds a notebook in her right hand and a staff in her left. Even her height will not stay still:
items.quote: At one moment it exceeded not the common height, at another her forehead seemed to strike the sky; and whenever she raised her head higher, she began to pierce within the very heavens, and to baffle the eyes of them that looked upon her.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 1, with James's note

items.title: Her torn robe
items.text: Her robe is torn, too. Violent hands have ripped it, each snatching what he could. Later she tells him who did it. After Socrates died, she says, the Epicureans, the Stoics and the rest each tried to seize what he left. They dragged her off as their prize:
items.quote: they tore in pieces the garment which I had woven with my own hands, and, clutching the torn pieces, went off, believing that the whole of me had passed into their possession.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 1 and prose 3

items.title: She raised him
items.text: She speaks to him like a nurse, in the old sense of the word: a woman who feeds a child and brings it up. She calls him her child. When he knows her at last, he calls her “my nurse, Philosophy, whose halls I had frequented from my youth up”. This is his way of saying he had studied philosophy since he was young. So in a sense she was with him all his life. She is the learning he had followed since his youth, come to find him in his cell. She asks him:
items.quote: Art thou that man, who, erstwhile fed with the milk and reared upon the nourishment which is mine to give, had grown up to the full vigour of a manly spirit?

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 2 and prose 3

items.title: What she teaches him
items.text: She treats him like a patient, one book at a time. In Book 2 she shows him that Fortune's gifts were never his to keep. In Book 3, that wealth, rank, power, fame and pleasure cannot make anyone happy. True happiness is God Himself. In Book 4, that the wicked only seem to win, for only the good have real power. In Book 5, that God knows what we will choose, and yet we choose freely. But first, in Book 1, she finds the root of his sickness:
items.quote: Thou hast ceased to know thy own nature.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 6; James's summaries of Books 2 to 5; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

items.title: After him
items.text: Readers kept her alive for centuries. The Old English version, whose preface names King Alfred, has the prisoner know her as “his own mother, that same Philosophy that long before had trained and taught him”. Dante found her too. When Beatrice died, he lost what he called “the chief delight of my Soul”. For comfort he turned to Boethius's book, though he found it hard at first. Reading it, he came to love Philosophy herself, “the Lady of these authors, of these sciences, and of these books”. Like Boethius, he pictured her as a woman:
items.quote: I imagined her in the form of a gentle Lady; and I could imagine her in no other attitude than a compassionate one.

cite.text: The Old English Boethius, tr. Sedgefield (1900); Dante, The Banquet, the second treatise, tr. Sayer (1887); Catholic Encyclopedia

extras.title: His prison book
extras.lede: He wrote The *Consolation of Philosophy* in his cell. It is a dialogue in five short books, prose and poems in turn. Gibbon called it “a golden volume not unworthy of the leisure of Plato or Tully”. Tully is Cicero.

items.title: A doctor at his bedside
items.text: It opens with him in tears, writing sad verses with the Muses of poetry at his bed. Then a woman appears above him: Lady Philosophy. She drives the Muses out, and spends five books talking him back to sense. He wrote himself as the patient. Her first words are for the Muses.
items.quote: Who has allowed yon play-acting wantons to approach this sick man—these who, so far from giving medicine to heal his malady, even feed it with sweet poison?

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 1

items.title: Fortune's wheel
items.text: Philosophy lets Fortune speak for herself. Why complain, Fortune asks, when she only takes back what was never his? Rising and falling is her game, and she never stops playing it.
items.quote: I turn the wheel that spins. I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 2

items.title: God's knowledge and our freedom
items.text: The last book asks a hard question. If God knows what we will choose, are we free? Philosophy answers that God sees all of time at once. So His knowing is “not foreknowledge as of something future, but knowledge of a moment that never passes”. Seeing a thing happen does not force it to happen. Medieval writers on God and time started from his definition of eternity.
items.quote: Now, eternity is the possession of endless life whole and perfect at a single moment.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 5, prose 6; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

items.title: Plato in a Christian's book
items.text: Philosophy teaches some of Plato's ideas. One poem says all learning is remembering what the soul knew before, with a hedge: “If Plato's teaching erreth not, / We learn but that we have forgot.” Another follows Plato's Timaeus, James notes, down to a world-soul “of threefold nature, moving all”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* finds “evident traces of the influence of the Neo-Platonists” in the book, and little that is Christian. His Loeb translators disagree:
items.quote: The development of the argument is anything but Neoplatonic; it is all his own.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 3, poems 9 and 11; Catholic Encyclopedia; Stewart and Rand

items.title: Why no Christ?
items.text: The book never names Christ. Hodgkin wrote in 1886 that “the name of Christ is never once mentioned, the tone, though religious and reverential, is that of a Theist only”. Some critics said Boethius was no Christian, or gave up his faith in prison. But Cassiodorus, who knew him, lists his Christian works: “He wrote a book concerning the Holy Trinity, and certain dogmatic chapters, and a book against Nestorius.” His Loeb translators explain the silence:
items.quote: In the Consolation he is writing philosophy; in the Tractates he is writing theology.

cite.text: Hodgkin, The Letters of Cassiodorus; Catholic Encyclopedia; Stewart and Rand, Introduction

items.title: Its last words
items.text: The book ends with Philosophy's charge to live well, since God sees all we do.
items.quote: Great is the necessity of righteousness laid upon you if ye will not hide it from yourselves, seeing that all your actions are done before the eyes of a Judge Who seeth all things.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 5, prose 6

words.note: Most of these lines come from the *Consolation*, the dialogue he wrote in prison. In it the prisoner, Boethius himself, complains, and Lady Philosophy answers. Each line says who speaks. The *Consolation* is in H. R. James's translation of 1897.

feature.kicker: In prison, remembering his sons' great day
feature.q: For truly in adverse fortune the worst sting of misery is to have been happy.
feature.ctx: The prisoner speaks: Boethius himself, after Philosophy has listed all his blessings. In Latin, {la|Nam in omni aduersitate fortunae infelicissimum est genus infortunii fuisse felicem.}

cite.text: Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2, prose 4

quotes.q: Sovereign Ruler, Lord of all! / Can it be that Thou disdainest / Only man? ’Gainst him, poor thrall, / Wanton Fortune plays her vainest. / Guilt’s deserved punishment / Falleth on the innocent.
quotes.who: The prisoner, to God, in his cell. James titles the poem Boethius' Prayer.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, poem 5

quotes.q: If God exists, whence comes evil? Yet whence comes good, if He exists not?
quotes.who: The prisoner, quoting an unnamed philosopher, as he asks why God lets the wicked win

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 4

quotes.q: For truly I believe that Ill Fortune is of more use to men than Good Fortune.
quotes.who: Philosophy. Good Fortune lies, she says, and Ill Fortune tells the truth: “The one deceives, the other teaches.”

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 8

quotes.q: Cease, then, to seek the wealth thou hast lost, since in true friends thou hast found the most precious of all riches.
quotes.who: Philosophy. His fall had shown him who his real friends were.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 8

quotes.q: What law can lovers move? A higher law is love!
quotes.who: Philosophy, in a poem about Orpheus, who turned back for Eurydice at the gates of hell and lost her

cite.text: Consolation, Book 3, poem 12

quotes.q: The individual substance of a rational nature.
quotes.who: His definition of a person, in his own voice. The medieval schools took it up, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. Tr. Stewart and Rand, 1918.

cite.text: Against Eutyches and Nestorius, chapter 3

myths.claim: Dante first had the thought: “There is no greater sorrow / Than to be mindful of the happy time / In misery.”
myths.truth: Dante wrote those words, but the thought is older. In prison Boethius wrote that “the worst sting of misery is to have been happy”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* calls Dante's lines “a haunting memory of Boethius”.

cite.text: Dante, Inferno, Canto 5; Consolation, Book 2, prose 4; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: “There is nothing either good or bad but thinking makes it so” is a line of Boethius.
myths.truth: It is Hamlet's. H. R. James borrowed Hamlet's words when he translated Boethius in 1897: “nothing is wretched, but thinking makes it so”. The Latin is plainer: {la|nihil est miserum nisi cum putes}, nothing is wretched unless you think it so.

cite.text: Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 2, scene 2; Consolation, Book 2, prose 4

myths.claim: The Latin proverb {la|Si tacuisses, philosophus mansisses} (if you had kept silent, you would have stayed a philosopher) is his.
myths.truth: Only the first half. In his book, a vain man is told he will prove himself a philosopher if he bears insults patiently. He bears them, then boasts of it. His critic retorts: “I should have hadst thou held thy peace.” The Latin there is {la|si tacuisses}. The words about staying a philosopher are not in his book.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 7, in English and in Latin

myths.claim: He invented the wheel of Fortune.
myths.truth: No. Cicero speaks of Fortune's wheel, {la|fortunae rotam}, in a speech nearly six centuries earlier. Boethius gave it a voice. His Fortune says, “I turn the wheel that spins.” Medieval copies of his book often paint it.

cite.text: Cicero, Against Piso; Consolation, Book 2, prose 2

myths.claim: Gibbon called him “the last of the Romans”.
myths.truth: With a catch: “the last of the Romans whom Cato or Tully could have acknowledged for their countryman”. His Loeb translators put it another way: “Boethius was the last of the Roman philosophers, and the first of the scholastic theologians.”

cite.text: Gibbon, The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 39; Stewart and Rand, Introduction

stood.lede: Two of these lines are his own, from his short works on God. Three come from the *Consolation*, where Lady Philosophy answers him: he wrote them, but he gave them to her.

learning.place: Tractate 2, to John the Deacon, the last lines

mystery.place: On the Trinity, the first words

circle.name: Symmachus
circle.text: His father-in-law, who raised him. In the prison book Philosophy calls him “a man whose splendid character does honour to the human race”. Soon after Boethius died, the king had Symmachus brought to Ravenna and killed too.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 4; Anonymus Valesianus, section 92

circle.name: Rusticiana
circle.text: His wife, Symmachus's daughter. Procopius remembers her as “a woman who was always lavishing her wealth upon the needy”. Years later, when the Goths took Rome, she was reduced to begging for bread. The Goths accused her of destroying Theodoric's statues, to avenge her father and her husband, and wanted her killed. King Totila protected her.

cite.text: Procopius, History of the Wars, Book 7, chapter 20

circle.name: His sons, Symmachus and Boethius
circle.text: Made consuls together in 522, while still young. After Theodoric died, his daughter gave back to the children of Symmachus and Boethius their fathers' estates.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 2, prose 3; Procopius, History of the Wars, Book 5, chapter 2

circle.name: John the Deacon
circle.text: A friend in the Church. Boethius sent him three of his short works of theology, one of them “to his saintly master and reverend father John the Deacon”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says he was afterwards Pope John I.

cite.text: Theological Tractates 2, 3 and 5; Catholic Encyclopedia

circle.name: Albinus
circle.text: The senator accused of writing to the emperor against Theodoric. Boethius defended him, and fell with him.

cite.text: Anonymus Valesianus, sections 85 and 86

circle.name: Cyprian
circle.text: The official who accused Albinus, then brought false witnesses against Boethius too.

cite.text: Anonymus Valesianus, sections 85 and 86

circle.name: Basil, Opilio and Gaudentius
circle.text: Men he names among his accusers. Basil had been dismissed from the king's household and was driven by his debts. The king had sentenced the other two to banishment for various crimes. On the very day he ordered them out of Ravenna, they laid their charge against him.

cite.text: Consolation, Book 1, prose 4

circle.name: Theodoric
circle.text: The Ostrogothic king of Italy, an Arian Christian. He trusted Boethius for years, then had him condemned unheard and killed. Procopius says he wept over it before he died.

cite.text: Anonymus Valesianus, sections 86 and 87; Procopius, History of the Wars, Book 5, chapter 1

circle.name: Cassiodorus
circle.text: A fellow statesman and a relative. He drafted the king's letters to Boethius. A note of his confirms that the Christian treatises are Boethius's own.

cite.text: Cassiodorus, Variae; Hodgkin, The Letters of Cassiodorus; Stewart and Rand, Introduction

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: They never met. Boethius hoped his book on the Trinity would show “the seeds sown in my mind by St. Augustine's writings”. Today they lie in the same church at Pavia.

cite.text: On the Trinity, preface; Orthodox Encyclopedia

death.big: He was put to death near Pavia in 524, or perhaps 526, on King Theodoric's orders. He was never given a hearing.
paras: A short chronicle by an unknown writer of the sixth century tells how he died. It turns against the king in his last years. It says the king had him killed on the estate where he was held, usually taken to be Calvenzano, near Pavia. “He was tortured for a long time with a cord bound about his forehead so tightly that his eyes cracked in their sockets, and finally, while under torture, he was beaten to death with a cudgel.” No last words are recorded.

The king then had Symmachus brought to Ravenna and put to death on a false charge. He feared that grief for his son-in-law would turn Symmachus against him. Pope John I came back from a mission to Constantinople. The king treated him as an enemy, and he died a few days later.

Procopius tells what happened next. A few days after the killings, a great fish's head was served to Theodoric at dinner. “This seemed to Theoderic to be the head of Symmachus newly slain.” He ran to his room, shivering, and lay under a heap of covers. He told his doctor, wept for the wrong he had done Symmachus and Boethius, and died not long after. Procopius calls the killings the king's “first and last act of injustice” to his subjects.

later.title: A later story
later.text: Later tellings differ. Gibbon has him writing his book “in the tower of Pavia”. The 1883 decree says he was shut in a tower and killed with the sword. The sixth-century chronicle mentions neither: only a baptistery, an estate, a cord and a club.

cite.text: Gibbon, chapter 39; Acta Sanctae Sedis 16 (1883); Anonymus Valesianus, section 87

saint.big: Yes, for Catholics, as a local saint. Pavia has long honoured him as a martyr, and Rome confirmed that in 1883. He is not in the Church's general calendar. The Orthodox, Anglicans and Lutherans do not count him a saint.

churches.note: Pavia's cult confirmed in 1883. In today's *Roman Martyrology* on 23 October
No feast. The *Orthodox Encyclopedia* calls him a saint of the Catholic Church
Not in Common Worship or Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022
Not in the Missouri Synod or ELCA calendars

paras: On 15 December 1883 the Congregation of Rites confirmed the cult Pavia had kept from time out of mind, and Pope Leo XIII ratified it the same day. The decree names him {la|servo Dei Severino Boetio, philosopho martyri sancto nuncupato}: the servant of God Severinus Boethius, philosopher and martyr, called a saint. Today's *Roman Martyrology* lists him on 23 October as a martyr. The English edition of 1916 does not. It says he wrote the *Consolation* in prison and served God with integrity until the king put him to death. Pope Benedict XVI came to honour his tomb in 2007.

Was he killed for his faith? The decree says so. It calls Theodoric a most zealous follower of the Arian heresy, {la|acerrimus, uti erat, Arianae haeresis sectator}, who set out to destroy three Catholic leaders: Pope John, Symmachus and Boethius. It adds that the king had him buried in secret, for fear Catholics would honour him as a martyr.

The sixth-century sources give other reasons. The chronicle says the charge was treason, over a letter to the emperor. Boethius himself names treason and sacrilege. A Catholic saints' site, santodelgiorno.it, says plainly that his execution had political motives. Three facts stand behind both views. Theodoric was an Arian Christian. The emperor Justin was pressing the Arians in the East. And Pope John died soon after Boethius, held by the king as an enemy.

quotes.q: There can be no reasonable doubt, then, that Boethius died a Christian, though it is not easy to show from documentary sources that he died a martyr for the Catholic Faith. The absence of documentary evidence does not, however, prevent us from giving due value to the constant tradition on this point.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, article on Boethius

quotes.q: Boethius was without doubt a Christian, a Doctor and perhaps a martyr.
quotes.who: H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand, his Loeb translators, 1918

cite.text: The Theological Tractates, Introduction

prayer.intro: He wrote this prayer for Lady Philosophy to sing, in Book 3 of the *Consolation*. After it, she shows him the highest good.
prayer.q: Oh, grant, almighty Father, / Grant us on reason's wing to soar aloft / To heaven's exalted height; grant us to see / The fount of good; grant us, the true light found, / To fix our steadfast eyes in vision clear / On Thee. Disperse the heavy mists of earth, / And shine in Thine own splendour. For Thou art / The true serenity and perfect rest / Of every pious soul—to see Thy face, / The end and the beginning—One the guide, / The traveller, the pathway, and the goal.

tidbits.text: A geometry book under his name shows Hindu-Arabic numerals, zero and all. If he wrote that passage, these numerals were in Europe by about 500. But the book was put together centuries later, and no reliable evidence shows he knew them.

cite.text: Smith and Karpinski, The Hindu-Arabic Numerals, 1911; Orthodox Encyclopedia

tidbits.text: Chaucer put his prison book into English, and so did Queen Elizabeth I. An Old English version is older still, and its preface says King Alfred the Great made it.

cite.text: W. J. Sedgefield, King Alfred's Version of the Consolations of Boethius, 1900

tidbits.text: He taught that music comes in three kinds. The first is the harmony of the universe, and the second the harmony within a human being. Only the third is music played on instruments.

cite.text: His book on music, Book 1, chapter 2; Orthodox Encyclopedia

tidbits.text: He took up a question the medieval schools argued over for centuries. Do kinds of things, like *animal* or *man*, exist in their own right, or only in the mind? His answer, following Aristotle: they exist in things, and the mind draws them out.

cite.text: Commentary on Porphyry, Book 1; Orthodox Encyclopedia
